questions.stem: About muscle in general:
options: It can only be stimulated by a nervous excitation
It contracts (shortens) under the influence of a stimulus
It is the driving element of the locomotor apparatus
The study of muscles is called myology
The study of muscles is called osteology
questions.explanation: Stimuli can be nervous, electrical, thermal, painful, etc. Osteology is the study of the skeleton.

questions.stem: Which of the following are roles of the muscular system?
questions.explanation: Roles: movement, thermogenesis, posture, joint stabilization, protection of viscera, visceral functions (digestion, urination, blood propulsion, childbirth…). Calcium storage and blood cell production are roles of bone.

questions.stem: Muscle tone (tonicity):
options: Allows balance to be maintained at rest (posture)
Is the ability to stretch without tearing
Is the ability to maintain a slight permanent contraction despite relaxation
questions.explanation: The ability to stretch without tearing is elasticity, a different property. Also false: "Persists when lying down"; "Is maximal in coma".

questions.stem: A muscle that stretches during passive movement of a joint without being torn is showing which property?
questions.explanation: Elasticity is the ability to stretch without tearing. Rigidity is not a muscle property.

questions.stem: Skeletal muscle:
options: Is controlled by the autonomic nervous system
Is also called striated or red muscle
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle fatigues fast; cardiac and visceral muscles never fatigue. Also false: "Has a slow, continuous contraction"; "Is controlled by the autonomic nervous system".

questions.stem: Cardiac muscle (myocardium):
options: Is classified as a mixed muscle
Is controlled by the central nervous system
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is controlled by the autonomic nervous system and never fatigues.

questions.stem: Visceral (smooth) muscle:
options: Is controlled by the autonomic nervous system
Is found in the walls of hollow viscera and vessels
questions.explanation: Muscles attached to the skeleton are skeletal (striated) muscles. Also false: "Is made of striated cells"; "Has a fast, rhythmic contraction".

questions.stem: Which muscle type is striated but involuntary?
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle has striated cells but is involuntary and automatic. Skeletal is striated and voluntary; visceral is smooth and involuntary.

questions.stem: About the number of skeletal muscles:
options: There are about 600 constant skeletal muscles
The plantaris muscle is an example of an inconstant muscle
Their number varies because of inconstant (accessory) muscles
The number of skeletal muscles never varies
questions.explanation: 600 constant skeletal muscles, plus inconstant accessory muscles such as the plantaris. 206 is the number of bones.

questions.stem: Superficial (supra-aponeurotic) muscles:
options: Are located deep to the aponeurosis
Include the muscles of the digestive and respiratory systems
Include the muscles of the sensory organs
questions.explanation: Superficial muscles are subcutaneous (facial muscles). Muscles of the digestive/respiratory systems, skeleton and sense organs are deep (sub-aponeurotic).

questions.stem: About the parts of a simple (monogastric) muscle:
options: It has a single belly between two tendons
The tendons are the contractile part
The tendons are narrow, whitish, elastic and resistant
It has two bellies and one intermediate tendon
The belly is large, red, fleshy and contractile
questions.explanation: A simple muscle has one belly (contractile) and two tendons. Two bellies with an intermediate tendon is a digastric muscle.

questions.stem: Match the muscle variety with its example:
questions.explanation: Rectus abdominis has several bellies in series with intermediate tendons (multigastric), not two parallel bellies (bifid). Also false: "Bifid muscle: the quadriceps femoris"; "Multifid muscle: the digastric muscle".

questions.stem: A muscle with several bellies arranged in parallel, whose parallel tendons are called heads, is:
questions.explanation: Multifid = several parallel bellies (e.g. quadriceps femoris). Bifid has two parallel bellies; multigastric has bellies in series.

questions.stem: About muscle insertions:
options: The origin can sometimes become mobile
The origin is usually distal and mobile
The termination is usually distal and mobile
The cricothyroid has a skin insertion
The palmaris brevis has a bony insertion
questions.explanation: The palmaris brevis is the example of a skin (cutaneous) insertion; bony insertion example: iliopsoas. Also false: "The origin is usually distal and mobile"; "The cricothyroid has a skin insertion".

questions.stem: Which muscle is given as the example of an aponeurotic insertion?
questions.explanation: Bone: iliopsoas; cartilage: cricothyroid; aponeurosis: abductor hallucis; skin: palmaris brevis.

questions.stem: Match the muscle shape with its example:
options: Geometric muscle: the muscles of the hypothenar compartment
questions.explanation: Short muscles are those of the hypothenar compartment; geometric muscles are the trapezius, pronator quadratus and depressor anguli oris.

questions.stem: Muscle nomenclature: match the criterion with the muscle name:
options: Number of heads criterion: triceps brachii
questions.explanation: Rectus abdominis and internal oblique are named after the direction of their fibres. Form: piriformis, quadratus plantaris; size: gluteus maximus, pectoralis minor.

questions.stem: About the muscle appendices:
options: Fibrous sheaths are sacs filled with synovial fluid
Tendinous serous sheaths are fibrous grooves forming osteofibrous canals
Serous (synovial) bursae are sacs filled with synovial fluid near joints that facilitate gliding
The muscular fascia encases and separates the muscles
questions.explanation: There are four appendices: serous bursae, tendinous serous sheaths, fibrous sheaths and muscular fascia. Also false: "Tendinous serous sheaths are fibrous grooves forming osteofibrous canals"; "Fibrous sheaths are sacs filled with synovial fluid".

questions.stem: About muscle exploration methods shown in the course:
options: The electromyogram (EMG) records the electrical activity of the muscle
CT and MRI can show the muscles of the thigh
A muscle biopsy is a muscle sample
Muscle testing is scored from 0 to 10
Muscle testing assesses the strength of a muscle on a scale from 0 to 5
questions.explanation: Muscle testing is scored from 0 to 5.

questions.stem: Match the muscle pathology with its definition:
options: Cramp: sudden, involuntary, painful and transient contraction that stops spontaneously
Bursitis: inflammation of the serous bursae
Compartment syndrome: rupture of a muscle after excessive stretching
Tenosynovitis: inflammation of the muscular fascia
Contracture: involuntary, painful and permanent contraction (e.g. torticollis)
questions.explanation: Tenosynovitis is inflammation of the synovial sheaths of tendons. Compartment syndrome is muscle ischemia from increased pressure in a compartment; rupture after excessive stretching is a tear (claquage).
